name: Kutep
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Koops, Robert. 2009. A grammar of Kuteb: A Jukunoid language of east-central Nigeria. Koeppe. Not online (also Koops 1990 diss.).

new_statements.quote: Although in terms of the world's tone languages, Kuteb is a 'register tone' language, as opposed to 'contour tone' languages, it will be seen that the limited tonal patterns on words make it a little like a contour tone language. [...] While there is some evidence for rhythmic patterns in Kuteb, they do not seem to be distinctive enough to base any rules or categories on. They seem rather to be a corollary of pitch patterns and morphological structure. This is an area that needs further inquiry, particularly with instruments.
new_statements.citation: Koops, Robert. 2007 [publ. 2009]. A grammar of Kuteb: A Jukunoid language of East-Central Nigeria. African Language Monographs I (KWEF), ed. R. Blench. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe. Pre-publication draft, December 2007.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 3 'Phonology Part II: Prosody', §3.2 'Tone Patterns' (draft p. 47, TOC pagination) and §3.3.2 'Rhythmic Patterns and the syllable' (draft p. 51); published 2009 pagination may differ slightly
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kuteb is a lexical register-tone language (low, mid, high; falling and rising glides; up-step and tone-spreading sandhi). The grammar makes no statement about word stress at all; the closest passage says that rhythmic (prominence) patterns are not distinctive and merely follow from pitch and morphology. No stress position can be assigned.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Vowel length is judged non-contrastive apart from a few ideophonic forms (§2.2.3, p. 25). Tone-pattern inventory: two-syllable words show only LL, LM, LH, HH, HM, HL, HF (§3.6.1, p. 59).
new_statements.domain_note: Word and phrase level tone; §3.6 posits a 'phonological word' as the unit of tone-pattern placement and leaves the phonological phrase for future research. Nothing on citation-form vs. connected-speech prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Koops' grammar is based mainly on the Lissam (Askaen) dialect, the author's field base since 1966 (e.g. 'I do not record double stops... for Lissam dialect', §2.1 p. 19; Welmers 1948 also worked on a Lissam subdialect); Koops groups Kuteb dialects as Bika-Kpambai, Lissam-Lumbu, Jenuwa-Fikyu-Kpambo and Rufun (§1.4, p. 10). Glottolog has no separate dialect codes under kute1248 that I saw; identity = kute1248.

Roger Blench. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe. Pre-publication Word draft dated December 2007, 312 pp. (published 2009 as xvi+287 pp., ISBN 978-3-89645-422-5).
sources.note: Ch. 2-3 (Phonology I: Segments, pp. 19-46; Phonology II: Prosody, pp. 47-60) describe Kuteb as a register tone language (low/mid/high plus falling and rising glides, up-step, tone sandhi). The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the 65,680-word text; 'accent' occurs once as 'acute accent' (tone diacritic). The only prominence-related remark is 3.3.2 (p. 51): rhythmic patterns exist but 'do not seem to be distinctive enough to base any rules or categories on' and are 'a corollary of pitch patterns and morphological structure'. Vowel length is not contrastive (2.2.3, p. 25). No word-stress…
